opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the time, I don't think any of us really expected what happened. Internally, it was framed as a low-key research preview. We had been working on the underlying models and the RLHF pipeline for a while, and the idea was more like: let's put this out there, see how people actually use a conversational interface, and collect feedback so we can find failure modes we couldn't find ourselves. There was even some debate about whether it was worth releasing at all, because the base capabilities weren't dramatically different from what was already available through the API.

From my side, I was mostly focused on the infrastructure, making the training and post-training systems run reliably and fast. So my mental model was very engineering-oriented: can we iterate quickly, can we scale it, will the servers hold up. I wasn't thinking, "this is going to change the world next week."

Then it launched, and within a few days the usage just exploded. The servers were struggling, everyone was scrambling, and it was clear we had dramatically underestimated how much the format mattered. The model itself wasn't a huge leap, but making it accessible through a simple chat window, free, where anyone could just talk to it, turned out to be the real unlock.

Looking back, I think the lesson for me was that product form and accessibility can matter as much as raw capability. You can have a strong model sitting behind an API, and only developers notice. Put it in front of ordinary people in a natural interface, and suddenly everyone understands what it can do. That experience changed how I think about the relationship between research and deployment.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the team wanted to see how people used the interface and collect feedback to uncover failure modes, which communicates gathering real-world user data.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the team did not expect the usage surge, but does not state that they expected initial interest to fade away.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, at the time, none of us thought it was going to be that big of a deal. Internally, ChatGPT was framed as a "low-key research preview." We had GPT-3.5 sitting there, we'd been doing a lot of work on instruction following and RLHF, and the question was really, how do we get this in front of more people so we can learn from real usage? The chat interface was almost a packaging decision. We thought it would make the model easier to interact with for people who weren't going to write prompts in a playground.

So the purpose, from my point of view as an engineer, was mostly about feedback and iteration. You can only learn so much from internal red teaming and benchmarks. We wanted to see how the model failed in the wild, what people actually asked it, where it hallucinated, where it refused things it shouldn't, and feed that back into training. It was supposed to be a data-gathering step before whatever came next, which everyone was much more focused on.

In terms of prospects, I remember people guessing maybe a few hundred thousand users would try it, and it would quietly inform the next release. Instead it hit a million users in five days, and suddenly my job became keeping the thing up. We were scaling inference, fighting capacity, dealing with traffic patterns nobody had planned for. That was when it sank in that the interface itself changed what people thought the technology was. The capability had existed for months. What changed was that anyone could have a conversation with it, and that made it real to them in a way an API never did.

Looking back, I think the lesson I took was that accessibility is part of the research. Putting a model in a form that millions of people can poke at tells you things about it, and about what people want from it, that you simply cannot discover any other way.

r001.rationale: It says the goal was to get ChatGPT in front of more people, learn from real usage, and gather data for feedback and training.

r002.rationale: The response expected a few hundred thousand users and a quiet contribution to the next release, but does not state that user interest would fade away.

astra-6.text:
At the time, we thought of it as a research preview—a way to put the model in people’s hands and learn from how they actually used it. The conversational format made it easier to explore what the model could do, ask follow-up questions, and give feedback when it got something wrong.

We were excited about the potential, but there was a lot of uncertainty. Would people find it useful? What uses would emerge that we hadn’t anticipated? What limitations would become more apparent? The release was a way to start answering those questions. We didn’t know how large the response would be.

r001.rationale: It says the release would put the model in people’s hands and let the team learn from how people actually used it, communicating collection of real-world usage data.

r002.rationale: It says the team did not know how large the response would be, but does not say they expected user interest to fade.
